title: The Complete Ireland Travel Guide
subtitle: Cliffs, castles and music-filled pubs across a small island built for slow, scenic travel
summary: How to plan an Ireland trip: whether to focus on Dublin, the southwest or the west coast, when to go for the best weather odds, what it costs, and a practical nine-day itinerary.

sections.title: How Ireland divides
body: Ireland genuinely divides into a compact set of regions, each with a distinct feel — its small size means a first trip can realistically cover several without feeling rushed.
**The east.** [[dublin|Dublin]] and [[kilkenny|Kilkenny]] — the capital's museums and pubs, and a genuinely well-preserved medieval town within easy reach.

**The southwest.** [[cork-cobh|Cork and Cobh]], [[killarney-ring-of-kerry|Killarney and the Ring of Kerry]] and the [[dingle-peninsula|Dingle Peninsula]] — Ireland's most famous scenic driving country, and genuinely the reason many people visit.
**The west.** [[cliffs-of-moher-burren|the Cliffs of Moher and the Burren]], [[galway|Galway]] and [[connemara|Connemara]] — dramatic Atlantic coastline and a genuinely lively university city.
**The northwest and islands.** [[donegal|Donegal]] and the [[aran-islands|Aran Islands]] are both genuinely spectacular but sit further off the classic first-timer route.
sections.note: Most first-time visitors genuinely combine [[dublin|Dublin]] with the southwest and west coasts in a single loop. Donegal and the Aran Islands are where a longer or second trip belongs.

list.title: If this is your first trip
list.text: [[dublin|Dublin]], genuinely the natural starting point, with world-class museums and the best transport links.

list.title: If you want the classic scenic drives
list.text: [[killarney-ring-of-kerry|Killarney and the Ring of Kerry]] plus the [[dingle-peninsula|Dingle Peninsula]], genuinely Ireland's most celebrated coastal driving country.

list.title: If you want dramatic cliffs in a shorter trip
list.text: [[cliffs-of-moher-burren|The Cliffs of Moher and the Burren]], genuinely reachable as a long day trip from Galway or Dublin.

list.title: If you want a lively, walkable city
list.text: [[galway|Galway]], genuinely famous for its music-filled streets and easy access to the west coast.

list.title: If you want real remoteness
list.text: The [[aran-islands|Aran Islands]], genuinely still Irish-speaking, reachable only by ferry or small plane.

list.title: If you want the far northwest's wild cliffs
list.text: [[donegal|Donegal]], home to Slieve League, genuinely among Europe's highest sea cliffs and far quieter than the southwest.

sections.title: Getting around: driving, trains, and one common mistake
body: Ireland's small size genuinely disguises how slow its roads actually are — a mix of rental car for the coast and train for the main towns is the standard approach.

**Rent a car for the west and southwest.** It's genuinely the most flexible way to see [[killarney-ring-of-kerry|the Ring of Kerry]], [[dingle-peninsula|Dingle]] and [[connemara|Connemara]] at your own pace.
**Don't underestimate driving times.** A route that looks like ninety minutes on a map can genuinely take three hours on narrow, winding coast roads.
**Take the train between the bigger towns.** [[dublin|Dublin]], [[cork-cobh|Cork]], [[galway|Galway]] and [[kilkenny|Kilkenny]] are genuinely well connected without a car.
**Book island ferries around the weather.** Sailings to the [[aran-islands|Aran Islands]] genuinely depend on conditions and can be cancelled at short notice.
**Drive on the left, and take single-track roads slowly.** Rural roads are genuinely narrower, and hedges taller, than most visitors expect.
sections.note: Book your rental car and west-coast accommodation well ahead for a June–August trip — Ireland's small hotel and guesthouse stock genuinely sells out early in peak season.

sections.title: When to go
body: Ireland's weather is famously changeable in every season, so 'the best time' is really about balancing crowds against the odds of a dry day. **May, June and September** generally work best.
**Late spring** brings genuinely the best odds of mild, dry weather with long daylight and thinner crowds than midsummer.
**Summer** is warmest and busiest, with the longest days — also genuinely the most expensive and crowded season, especially along the west coast.
**Early autumn** is a genuinely underrated window, often mild with noticeably fewer visitors than summer.
**Winter** brings short days and frequent rain, but is genuinely atmospheric, with cosy pubs, fewer crowds and lower prices.
sections.note: Pack a proper waterproof jacket regardless of when you go — a sunny forecast in Ireland genuinely offers no guarantee by the afternoon.

list.title: Four days: Dublin alone
list.text: [[dublin|Dublin]]'s museums, castle and pubs, genuinely enough for a satisfying short city break.
list.tip: Add a single day trip to [[kilkenny|Kilkenny]] by train if you have a fifth day free.

list.title: Nine days: the classic loop
list.text: The itinerary on the [[c:ireland|Ireland country page]]: [[dublin|Dublin]], [[kilkenny|Kilkenny]], [[cork-cobh|Cork]], [[killarney-ring-of-kerry|Killarney]], [[dingle-peninsula|Dingle]], [[cliffs-of-moher-burren|the Cliffs of Moher]] and [[galway|Galway]]. A genuinely complete first look at Ireland's classic highlights.
list.tip: Break up the longer driving days with an early start — west-coast light is genuinely best in the morning.

list.title: A week focused on the west coast
list.text: [[galway|Galway]], [[connemara|Connemara]] and [[cliffs-of-moher-burren|the Cliffs of Moher]] as a self-contained trip, skipping the long transit south.
list.tip: Base yourself in Galway and take day trips rather than changing accommodation each night.

list.title: A Donegal and Aran Islands add-on for a second trip
list.text: [[donegal|Donegal]]'s Slieve League cliffs and the [[aran-islands|Aran Islands]], genuinely two of Ireland's most remote and rewarding corners.
list.tip: Rent a bike on [[aran-islands|Inis Mór]] rather than joining a minibus tour for a genuinely slower, quieter visit.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Ireland?
faq.a: Nine to twelve days covers Dublin and a loop through the south and west coast at a reasonable pace, which is the itinerary in this guide. Four to five days is enough for Dublin and one nearby region, and genuinely still worthwhile on its own.

faq.q: Is the west coast worth the extra driving time?
faq.a: Yes, genuinely — the Ring of Kerry, Dingle and the Cliffs of Moher are a large part of why people visit, and the slower pace is part of the experience rather than a drawback.

faq.q: Do you need a car in Ireland?
faq.a: For the west and southwest coasts, yes, genuinely — though trains and buses cover Dublin, Cork, Galway and Kilkenny well without one.

faq.q: What is the best time of year to visit for good weather?
faq.a: May, June and September offer genuinely the best odds of mild, dry weather with thinner crowds than July and August, though no season in Ireland guarantees a dry day.
